title: Fast, non-cryptographic hashes for keys and buckets
description: Industry-standard, non-cryptographic hashes inside DuckDB SQL — [xxHash](https://cyan4973.github.io/xxHash/), [MurmurHash3](https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher), [RapidHash](https://github.com/Nicoshev/rapidhash), wyhash, komihash, SipHash, CRC-32C and FNV-1a — plus functions that reproduce BigQuery, Spark, Kafka, Iceberg and ClickHouse hashes exactly, and Jump consistent hashing. These are speed-first hashes: fast and well-distributed against random input, where the only "adversary" is randomness, not a person who controls the bytes. For digests, signatures, or HMAC, use the [crypto](/products/extensions/crypto) extension instead.

sections.title: What it is
sections.description: Hashfuncs gives you fast, deterministic 32-, 64-, and 128-bit hashes — the slot between DuckDB's built-in [`hash()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/utility) (great for join/group-by internals, but implementation-defined and unsafe to persist or reproduce elsewhere) and a cryptographic hash (an order of magnitude slower, and unnecessary when nothing adversarial is at stake). The natural workloads are partitioning, sharding, deduplication, cache keys, and probabilistic-filter inputs — anywhere you want a stable, well-distributed value derived from data at near-RAM bandwidth.

sections.title: Hashfuncs vs. crypto — picking the right extension
sections.description: These two extensions look similar but solve different problems. Pick by the threat model, not by output width.

bulletPoints.label: Use hashfuncs when speed wins
bulletPoints.description: Partitioning, sharding, deduplication, cache keys, [Bloom-filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom_filter) inputs — workloads where the adversary is randomness, not a human. `xxh3_64` and `rapidhash` run roughly an order of magnitude faster than SHA-256.

bulletPoints.label: Use crypto when collisions must be hard to forge
bulletPoints.description: Digital signatures, HMAC, content-addressed storage with adversarial input, tamper-evident audit logs, password salts, secure random bytes — anything an attacker could try to break. The [crypto](/products/extensions/crypto) extension gives you BLAKE3, SHA-2, SHA-3, HMAC, and a CSPRNG.

bulletPoints.label: Don't substitute one for the other
bulletPoints.description: These hashes are explicitly **not** collision-resistant against a motivated adversary. Treating an `xxh3_128` like a SHA-256 digest is a security bug, not a performance optimization. The inverse is also wrong: spending SHA-256 on partition routing is wasted CPU. (For password storage, neither family is the answer — use a real password hash like bcrypt or argon2 outside DuckDB.)

bulletPoints.label: They compose
bulletPoints.description: Both extensions can be loaded together. A common pattern: [`crypto`](/products/extensions/crypto) for the durable identity hash on a row, `hashfuncs` for the routing hash that decides which shard processes it.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: Every function is a scalar SQL function: the value, plus an optional seed (or key). Each algorithm is an upstream-faithful C/C++ implementation linked into the extension binary: no catalog, no secrets, no network, every call pure CPU.

bulletPoints.label: Many algorithms, one interface
bulletPoints.description: [xxHash](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash) (32 / 64 / 128-bit, including a hex digest; XXH3 variants are tuned for SSE2 / AVX2 / NEON), [MurmurHash3](https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher) (32-bit plus x86 and x64 128-bit forms), [RapidHash](https://github.com/Nicoshev/rapidhash), wyhash, komihash, keyed SipHash, CRC-32C and FNV-1a. Every function accepts booleans, numbers, `DECIMAL`, dates and timestamps, `INTERVAL`, `UUID`, `ENUM`, `VARCHAR` and `BLOB` — and unsupported types are rejected when the query is planned, not halfway through it.

bulletPoints.label: Row hashing for multi-column keys
bulletPoints.description: Pass a tuple, struct, list, map or array — `xxh3_64((a, b, c))` — and the whole value is hashed through one documented, unambiguous encoding. Unlike concatenating strings, `('a|', 'b')` and `('a', '|b')` hash differently, and `NULL` fields are distinguished from empty ones.

bulletPoints.label: Exact matches for other systems
bulletPoints.description: `farm_fingerprint` returns BigQuery's `FARM_FINGERPRINT`, `spark_hash` and `spark_xxhash64` return Spark's `hash()` and `xxhash64()` (including Spark's type rules), `kafka_partition` returns the partition Kafka's default partitioner picks, `iceberg_bucket` returns Iceberg's `bucket[N]` partition, and `clickhouse_cityhash64` returns ClickHouse's `cityHash64`. Each is tested against values produced by the real system.

bulletPoints.label: Consistent hashing for resharding
bulletPoints.description: `jump_hash(xxh3_64(key), n)` assigns keys to `n` shards so that adding a shard moves only about 1/(n + 1) of the keys, instead of nearly all of them with `hash % n`.

bulletPoints.label: Optional seeds for independent hash spaces
bulletPoints.description: Every function has a seeded overload. Two different seeds give two *uncorrelated* hash spaces from the same column — exactly what you need for double-hashing in [Bloom filters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom_filter) or running two parallel shardings whose bucket assignments must not correlate.

bulletPoints.label: Canonical hex digest for cross-language reproducibility
bulletPoints.description: The 128-bit xxHash variant can emit the lowercase 32-character canonical hex form defined in the [xxHash specification](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/blob/dev/doc/xxhash_spec.md), in `high64 || low64` byte order. That digest matches what [Python xxhash](https://pypi.org/project/xxhash/), [xxhash-rust](https://docs.rs/xxhash-rust/latest/xxhash_rust/), and `XXH128_canonicalFromHash` in C produce over the same bytes — so a fingerprint round-trips across SQL and application code.

bulletPoints.label: Feeds the bitfilters extension directly
bulletPoints.description: The 64-bit `UBIGINT`-returning hashes (`xxh3_64`, `rapidhash`) are the natural input to the [bitfilters](/products/extensions/bitfilters) extension's Bloom, XOR, Quotient, and Binary Fuse filters — sub-microsecond probabilistic set-membership built entirely in one DuckDB session.
